subject: chemistry
promptStrong: Give me a challenging GCSE exam-style question on strong and weak acids and titration, then mark my answer against the Eduqas spec.
promptWeak: Explain strong and weak acids and pH for GCSE Eduqas Chemistry simply, with a worked example and the most common mistake.

questions.q: Which set of substances all react with dilute acids?
questions.explain: Acids react with some metals (giving a salt + hydrogen), with bases including alkalis (salt + water) and with carbonates (salt + water + carbon dioxide).

questions.q: Predict the products when dilute hydrochloric acid reacts with magnesium.
questions.explain: Acid + metal gives a salt plus hydrogen: Mg + 2HCl -> MgCl2 + H2. The salt of hydrochloric acid is a chloride.

questions.q: What is the correct test to confirm that a gas is carbon dioxide?
options: It gives a squeaky pop with a lit splint
questions.explain: Carbon dioxide turns limewater milky/cloudy. Relighting a glowing splint tests for oxygen; the squeaky pop tests for hydrogen.

questions.q: You add dilute acid to an unknown white solid and it fizzes, producing a gas that turns limewater milky. Which ion is present?
questions.explain: Carbonates react with dilute acid to release carbon dioxide, which turns limewater milky. This is the standard test for carbonate ions.

questions.q: When an acid dissolves in water, which ion does it form?
questions.explain: Acids form hydrogen ions (H+) in water. Solutions of alkalis contain hydroxide ions (OH-).

questions.q: Which statement about the pH scale is correct?
options: pH below 7 is acidic and above 7 is alkaline
The pH scale only measures alkalis
questions.explain: pH measures acidity/alkalinity: below 7 is acidic, 7 is neutral, above 7 is alkaline. pH can be measured with an indicator chart or a digital pH meter.

questions.q: What is produced when an acid is neutralised by a base that is not a carbonate?
options: A salt plus carbon dioxide only
questions.explain: Neutralisation of an acid by a base forms a salt plus water. With a carbonate you also get carbon dioxide.

questions.q: Which salt is formed when sulfuric acid reacts with copper(II) oxide?
questions.explain: Sulfuric acid always forms a sulfate salt. CuO + H2SO4 -> CuSO4 + H2O, so copper(II) sulfate is produced.

questions.q: When preparing a soluble salt from an insoluble base, why is excess base added to the warm acid?
options: To change the salt into a gas
To lower the pH of the solution
To make sure all the acid has reacted
questions.explain: Excess insoluble base ensures all the acid is neutralised. The unreacted excess is then removed by filtration before the solution is crystallised.

questions.q: In the preparation of crystals of a soluble salt from an insoluble carbonate, what is the correct final step to obtain crystals?
options: Boil the solution completely dry as fast as possible
Filter off the salt while it is still hot
Evaporate some water then leave to crystallise slowly
Add more acid until crystals appear
questions.explain: The filtrate is evaporated to concentrate it, then left to cool so crystals form slowly. Boiling completely dry gives a powder, not well-formed crystals.

questions.q: In a titration to prepare a soluble salt from an alkali, why is an indicator used?
options: To show the exact end point of neutralisation
questions.explain: The indicator changes colour at the end point, showing when the acid has exactly neutralised the alkali so the correct volume can be recorded.

questions.q: In specified practical SP7B, a strong acid is titrated against a strong base. Which piece of apparatus delivers an accurately measured, variable volume of acid?
questions.explain: A burette delivers accurate, variable volumes and is read to the nearest 0.05 cm3. A pipette measures a fixed volume; the conical flask holds the solution being titrated.

questions.q: The terms 'dilute' and 'concentrated' describe which property of an acid?
options: The degree of ionisation of the acid
The amount of acid dissolved in a given volume
questions.explain: Dilute and concentrated refer to the amount of substance (moles) of acid dissolved in a given volume of solution, not to how fully the acid ionises.

questions.q: What distinguishes a strong acid from a weak acid?
options: A strong acid is always more concentrated
A strong acid is fully ionised in water; a weak acid is only partially ionised
A strong acid never reacts with metals
A weak acid contains no hydrogen ions
questions.explain: Strong and weak describe the degree of ionisation. A strong acid ionises completely in water; a weak acid ionises only partially. This is separate from concentration.

questions.q: Equal concentrations of a strong acid and a weak acid are each reacted with magnesium ribbon. What is observed with the strong acid compared with the weak acid?
options: Exactly the same rate of reaction
questions.explain: At equal concentration the strong acid has a higher hydrogen ion concentration, so it reacts faster and more vigorously with magnesium than the weak acid.

questions.q: Which ionic equation represents all aqueous neutralisation reactions?
questions.explain: All aqueous neutralisations can be generalised to hydrogen ions reacting with hydroxide ions to form water: H+ + OH- -> H2O.

questions.q: As the hydrogen ion concentration of a solution increases by a factor of ten, how does the pH change?
questions.explain: The pH scale is such that a tenfold increase in hydrogen ion concentration lowers the pH by one (e.g. pH 3 to pH 2).

questions.q: 0.5 mol of sodium hydroxide is dissolved to make 2 dm3 of solution. What is the concentration in mol/dm3?
questions.explain: Concentration = moles / volume = 0.5 / 2 = 0.25 mol/dm3.

questions.q: 25.0 cm3 of NaOH is exactly neutralised by 25.0 cm3 of 0.10 mol/dm3 HCl. The reaction is 1:1 (HCl + NaOH -> NaCl + H2O). What is the concentration of the NaOH?
questions.explain: Moles HCl = 0.10 x (25.0/1000) = 0.0025 mol. The 1:1 ratio gives 0.0025 mol NaOH in 25.0 cm3, so concentration = 0.0025 / 0.025 = 0.10 mol/dm3.

questions.q: Which reagent is used to test for aqueous sulfate ions?
questions.explain: Sulfate ions are identified by adding barium chloride solution (usually with dilute acid), giving a white precipitate of barium sulfate.
